ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — Julius Caesar

code.originalText: Urgent visit after a witnessed collapse with jerking and confusion, the third spell in eighteen months: history, examination, ECG, tests, cardiac monitor, seizure safety, and neurology referral

text.paragraph: Urgent visit after a witnessed collapse with jerking and confusion, the third spell in eighteen months: history, examination, ECG, tests, cardiac monitor, seizure safety, and neurology referral [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: Six days ago he collapsed at a long outdoor ceremony after a strange rising feeling, with jerking of both arms, a bitten tongue, and twenty minutes of confusion; it is his third spell in eighteen months, and he wants to know why he collapses and whether it will happen again in public. [S]
He wants to keep working, travelling, speaking, and riding. [S]
He is frustrated at being told not to drive. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Gaius Julius Caesar was born on 12 or 13 July 100 BC in the Subura district of Rome, into the patrician family of the Julii. [D]
Suetonius writes that he lost his father 'in the course of his sixteenth year'. [D]
Pliny the Elder records that two men of the family, one of them his father, a former praetor, 'died without any apparent cause, in the morning, while putting on their shoes'. [D]
As a young man, in hiding from Sulla's agents, he was 'suffering from a severe attack of quartan ague' and changed his hiding place almost every night. [D]

Plutarch describes him as 'of a spare habit', with 'a soft and white skin', and says he 'suffered from distemper in the head, and was subject to epileptic fits', the first of which attacked him at Corduba; he made 'his military service a cure for his feeble health'. [D]

Suetonius says he was tall, of sound health, 'except that towards the end he was subject to sudden fainting fits and to nightmare as well', and that he was 'twice attacked by the falling sickness' (comitialis morbus) during his campaigns. [D]

Plutarch gives a second account of the battle of Thapsus in Africa in 46 BC, in which 'his usual sickness laid hold of him' as he was drawing up his army, and, sensing it coming, he was carried to a nearby tower and stayed there during the battle. [D]
He drank very little wine: 'not even his enemies denied' it. [D]
His only daughter, Julia, died in childbirth in 54 BC. [D]
After the African campaign he returned to Rome in July 46 BC, celebrated four triumphs within a single month, and left Rome for Further Spain early in November 46 BC. [D]

He reformed the Roman calendar, which had drifted so far that the harvest festivals no longer came in summer, to a year of 365 days with a day added every fourth year; to realign it he lengthened 46 BC to 445 days, and the new calendar took effect on 1 January 45 BC. [D]

Retrospective readings take the attacks as epilepsy: one review counts four attacks that were probably complex partial (focal impaired-awareness) seizures and suggests an inherited cause; another treats them as late-onset epilepsy beginning at about 54 and proposes neurocysticercosis. [R]

Galassi and Ashrafian (2015) argued that his symptoms (headache, vertigo, falls, limb weakness, the collapse at Thapsus, and the giddiness at the Senate) fit cerebrovascular disease with transient ischemic attacks better than epilepsy, and that the sudden deaths in his family suggest cardiovascular disease. [R]
Other proposed causes include a brain arteriovenous malformation, a brain tumor such as a meningioma, celiac disease, and malaria. [R]

text.paragraph: Positive for the concerns in the history of present illness. Alert, articulate, and composed; oriented; full recall of events before and after the spell but none of the spell itself; mood "impatient to get back to work"; PHQ-9 3; no thoughts of self-harm. Neurological examination: fluent speech with normal naming and repetition; visual fields full; no pronator drift; normal strength, sensation, reflexes, coordination, and gait; healed bite on the left side of the tongue; no orthostatic drop in blood pressure. No other systems reported as affected in this synthetic episode. [S]

Work-up of transient loss of consciousness: witness account, orthostatic vital signs, 12-lead ECG today, a 14-day ambulatory ECG patch from tomorrow, blood count, electrolytes, calcium, glucose, kidney and liver tests, HbA1c, lipids, and TSH; EEG and MRI of the brain with diffusion-weighted and epilepsy-protocol sequences; CT angiography of the head and neck; transthoracic echocardiogram. Guideline: Evidence-based guideline: Management of an unprovoked first seizure in adults: Report of the Guideline Development Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology and the American Epilepsy Society (2015); 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Syncope (2017); 2021 Guideline for the Prevention of Stroke in Patients With Stroke and Transient Ischemic Attack (2021) [S]

Neurology consultation: is this epilepsy, syncope, or transient ischemic attack; review of the EEG, MRI, and vascular imaging; whether to start an antiseizure medicine and which; stroke prevention; and driving. Guideline: Evidence-based guideline: Management of an unprovoked first seizure in adults: Report of the Guideline Development Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology and the American Epilepsy Society (2015); Operational classification of seizure types by the International League Against Epilepsy: Position Paper of the ILAE Commission for Classification and Terminology (2017) [S]

Seizure safety from today: no driving until a seizure-free period set by state law and his neurologist; showers rather than baths; no swimming or riding alone; no climbing to heights; regular sleep of at least seven hours; a written seizure action plan for his staff, including when to call emergency services. Guideline: Evidence-based guideline: Management of an unprovoked first seizure in adults: Report of the Guideline Development Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology and the American Epilepsy Society (2015) [S]

Blood pressure: lisinopril 10 mg daily from today; home blood pressure log twice daily; potassium and creatinine in two weeks; target below 130/80 mmHg. Guideline: 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (2025); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, stroke and transient ischemic attack, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia monographs (2026) [S]

Lifestyle: Mediterranean-style diet with sodium below 2.3 g a day; aerobic activity at least 150 minutes a week; alcohol kept at his present low level; no tobacco. Guideline: 2021 Guideline for the Prevention of Stroke in Patients With Stroke and Transient Ischemic Attack (2021); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, stroke and transient ischemic attack, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia monographs (2026) [S]
